--- title: "Application exercise 4: Tuning K, and what scaling does" subtitle: "STA 363 | Meeting 4 | September 4" toc-depth: 2 execute: echo: true editor: source jupyter: python3 --- ## Setup ::: {#5f298e97 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt DATA = "https://lucymcgowan.github.io/sta-363-f26/data/" from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline Default = pd.read_csv(DATA + "Default.csv") X = Default[["balance", "income"]] y = (Default["default"] == "Yes").astype(int) X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split( X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=363, stratify=y ) float(round(y_test.mean(), 4)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 0.0333 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.question} That number is the proportion of the test set that defaulted. If you predicted "no default" for every single person, what would your error rate be? Write it down. It is the bar every model today has to clear. ::: ::: {.answer-space} ::: ## Part 1: Forget to scale ::: {#cbc9e07b .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} unscaled = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=25).fit(X_train, y_train) float(round(1 - unscaled.score(X_test, y_test), 4)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 0.0333 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#750a1e5b .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} scaled = make_pipeline( StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=25) ).fit(X_train, y_train) float(round(1 - scaled.score(X_test, y_test), 4)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` 0.0263 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.question} 1. Which did better? 2. The unscaled error should look familiar. Compare it to the number you wrote down above. What is the unscaled model actually predicting? ::: ::: {.answer-space} ::: Now look at the units. ::: {#5f204a79 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} X.describe().loc[["min", "max", "std"]].round(1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
balance income
min 0.0 772.0

std 483.7 13336.6
``` ::: ::: ::: {.question} Two customers differ by \$1,000 in `balance` and \$1,000 in `income`. Before scaling, how much does each difference contribute to the distance between them? Which predictor is deciding who counts as a neighbor? ::: ::: {.answer-space} ::: ## Part 2: Sweep K ::: {#be37f305 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} ks = [1, 3, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 200, 500] train_err, test_err = [], [] for k in ks: m = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=k)) m.fit(X_train, y_train) train_err.append(1 - m.score(X_train, y_train)) test_err.append(1 - m.score(X_test, y_test)) pd.DataFrame({"K": ks, "train": train_err, "test": test_err}).round(4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}
K train test

``` ::: ::: ::: {.question} 1. What is the training error at $K = 1$? Why is that value guaranteed before you run anything? 2. Which $K$ minimizes test error? 3. What happens to test error at very large $K$, and why? ::: ::: {.answer-space} ::: Plot it against $1/K$ so that flexibility increases left to right. ::: {#8adbb622 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5)) ax.plot([1 / k for k in ks], train_err, "-o", color="#595959", label="Training") ax.plot([1 / k for k in ks], test_err, "-o", color="#d5008f", label="Test") ax.set_xscale("log") ax.set_xlabel("1/K") ax.set_ylabel("Error rate") ax.legend() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](04-ex_files/figure-html/cell-7-output-1.png){} ::: ::: ::: {.question} Compare the shape of your curves to Figure 2.17 in the textbook. Where do they agree, and where does real data refuse to look like the textbook? ::: ::: {.answer-space} ::: ## Part 3: The error rate is hiding something The bank cannot contact everyone. Suppose they will reach out to the 100 customers the model considers most at risk. ::: {#cb455146 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} best = make_pipeline( StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=25) ).fit(X_train, y_train) probs = best.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1] top100 = np.argsort(-probs)[:100] float(round(y_test.values[top100].mean(), 3)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ``` 0.51 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.question} 1. What fraction of the top 100 actually defaulted? 2. Compare that to the overall default rate in the test set. How many times better than random is the model at finding defaulters? 3. The model's error rate was only slightly better than "predict no for everyone." Yet this number is dramatically better than chance. How can both be true? ::: ::: {.answer-space} ::: ::: {.takeaway} A classifier that is mediocre at *labelling* can be excellent at *ranking*. On October 2 we will replace the error rate with measures that can tell the difference. ::: ## If you finish early Add `student` as a third predictor.
